title: Elizabeth Ann Seton (1774–1821)
hookLine: a widowed mother, a convert, a founder of schools, honored as a saint

lines: A CATHOLIC FAMILY TAKES HER IN.
cards: Her husband coughs through the night in a cold stone quarantine building on the coast of Italy, and she is the one nursing him. He is dying of tuberculosis.

Their little daughter is with her; the other children are home in New York. She is American, an Episcopalian who reads her Bible. When her husband dies, an Italian Catholic family, the Filicchis, take her in.
She goes to Mass with them and watches how they pray. Then she sails home a widow, with young children, little money, and a head full of questions. Her name is Elizabeth Ann Seton.

teach.b: First, the turn. Back in New York, what drew her most was the Eucharist, the Catholic belief that Christ is truly present in the bread at Mass. She wrote about wanting to be near it.
She was received into the Catholic Church, and friends and relatives pulled away. Help dried up. Second, the classroom.
A widow with children had to earn a living, so she taught. A school she tried in New York struggled. Then she was invited to Baltimore, and opened a small school for girls.
Later, in a valley at Emmitsburg, Maryland, she started another, where poorer children could learn alongside those who paid. Third, the sisters.
Women came to join her, and she founded a religious community, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph's. They called her Mother Seton.
She was raising her own children through all of it, and she grieved the deaths of daughters she loved. Fourth, the saint.
The Church canonized her, and Catholic schools across the United States name her as a patron.

In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Suffer the little children, and forbid them not to come to me." She spent her last years doing that in a schoolroom, one lesson and one child at a time.

how: Catholics in the United States keep Elizabeth Ann Seton's feast in early January, and Catholic schools often mark it with a Mass and stories of her life; pilgrims visit her shrine at Emmitsburg, Maryland.

games.q: you've just become Catholic. friends and relatives pull away, money is short, and you have children to feed. what do you do?
o: go back to your old church to keep the peace.
teach. open a school and keep at it.
games.why: she taught. a school in New York struggled, then Baltimore, then Emmitsburg, where the Sisters of Charity began.

practice: Let one teacher come to mind: a schoolteacher, a coach, a grandmother at a kitchen table, a boss who showed you how. Remember one thing they taught you that you still use, and hold their face for a moment.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, simply stay with the gratitude.
